h1: The 8 Best 2-Bay NAS for Home Offices of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best 2-Bay NAS for Home Offices: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: the 8 best 2-bay NAS for home offices in 2026, from Synology and QNAP to UGREEN and Asustor, with picks for every budget.
summary: The Synology DS223 is the best 2-bay NAS for home offices because DSM is the easiest NAS software to learn. UGREEN's DXP2800 adds headroom for photo and video work, and the QNAP TS-264 includes 8GB of RAM for apps. TERRAMASTER offers quad-core Intel power, and the Synology DS725+ is the pick for growth.
intro: Buyers fixate on the box and forget the drives. Every NAS in this ranking ships diskless, so the real price is the enclosure plus two hard drives, and in RAID 1, where the drives mirror each other, you get the capacity of just one. Skimp on the drives and the best chassis in the world still gives you a slow, noisy, short-lived file server.

We reviewed eight 2-bay NAS units on paper, comparing software, networking, RAM, drive support and upgrade paths from the listings. Ranking leans on ease of use first, because in a small office the person administering the NAS is rarely a full-time IT worker. Hardware headroom comes second, with price tier as a check. Budget for two NAS-rated drives before you compare boxes.

products.name: Synology DS223 Home & Office Backup Hub (2-Bay Diskless NAS)
products.verdict: The easiest NAS software for first time buyers.
products.description:
The Synology DS223 is a 2-bay diskless NAS running DSM with RAID 1 support, in the $200 to $500 tier. It is a Value-series model with soldered RAM that cannot be upgraded, and it focuses on backup and basic surveillance monitoring. For many home offices, that is exactly the job: a place where laptops back up and files get shared with a couple of colleagues.

It ranks first because DSM is the easiest NAS software to learn, which counts for more than raw power in a small office. The QNAP and TERRAMASTER offer more RAM or CPU at similar money.

Buy it as a first NAS. The caveats are hardware: the RAM is soldered, so you cannot add memory later, and it is not built for running many apps. If you plan on containers or media servers, look at the QNAP TS-264.
products.skipIf: You want to run many apps.

products.name: UGREEN NAS DXP2800 2-Bay
products.verdict: More processing headroom for photo and video work.
products.description:
The UGREEN DXP2800 is a diskless 2-bay NAS running UGREEN NAS OS with RAID 1 support, built with content creator hardware in mind, in the $200 to $500 tier. Photo and video libraries are heavy on both storage and processing: thumbnails, indexing and previews all lean on the CPU, and extra headroom shows up as faster browsing.

It ranks second because that headroom helps media workflows, but UGREEN's software is newer than DSM, so the polish trails Synology. The listing also gives fewer spec numbers than some rivals, which makes it harder to compare on RAM or CPU.

Choose it if you handle large media files and want hardware first. Skip it if you want the most mature software. Drives are sold separately, so add them to the budget, and confirm the RAM and CPU on the manufacturer page.
products.skipIf: You want the most polished software.

products.name: QNAP TS-264-8G-US 2 Bay Desktop NAS
products.verdict: 8GB of RAM out of the box for running apps.
products.description:
The QNAP TS-264 is a 2-bay desktop NAS with 8GB of RAM included, QTS software, and multi-app and container support, in the $200 to $500 tier. RAM is the resource that apps consume first. Running a media server, a download manager and a backup service together eats memory quickly, and 8GB out of the box saves an upgrade.

It ranks third because the included RAM is a real advantage over the DS223's soldered chip, but QTS has a steeper learning curve than DSM. For a small office without a dedicated administrator, learning time counts.

Pick it if you will run several apps or media servers at once. Skip it if you only need backup, since the DS223 does that more easily. It is diskless, so you buy the drives separately, and containers add a layer of setup that beginners should expect.

products.name: TERRAMASTER F2-425 2-Bay NAS (Intel x86 Quad-Core)
products.verdict: Quad core Intel power with 2.5GbE and 4GB RAM.
products.description:
The TERRAMASTER F2-425 pairs an Intel x86 quad-core CPU with 4GB of RAM, 2.5GbE LAN and the TOS operating system in a 2-bay diskless chassis, in the $200 to $500 tier. An x86 processor matters because it runs a broad range of software and handles tasks like media transcoding better than lower-end chips.

It ranks fourth because the hardware is strong, yet TOS is less polished than DSM, and polish is what a small office values day to day. The 2.5GbE port moves files faster than gigabit, but only if your switch and computers support it.

Buy it if performance matters more than software finish and you are comfortable with a less refined interface. Skip it if you want simple software. Drives are sold separately, and the extra network speed is wasted on a gigabit-only network.

products.name: QNAP TS-216G-US 2-Bay 2.5GbE Desktop NAS
products.verdict: Faster networking if your switch supports it.
products.description:
The QNAP TS-216G is a 2-bay desktop NAS with 2.5GbE networking, QTS and RAID 1 support, diskless, in the $200 to $500 tier. The faster port is the point, since file transfers to a 2.5GbE-equipped computer can run beyond what a gigabit link allows.

It ranks below the TS-264 because the listing gives no RAM figure, so app headroom is unclear. You get the QTS ecosystem and fast networking, but you cannot tell whether it can handle containers. The TS-264 states 8GB.

Pick it if you already have a 2.5GbE switch and mainly want fast file access. Without a matching switch, the faster port goes unused. Check the RAM and CPU on the maker's page, and remember that drives are sold separately.

products.name: UGREEN NAS DH2300 2-Bay Desktop NAS (Diskless)
products.verdict: Supports up to 64TB total capacity at a low price.
products.description:
The UGREEN DH2300 is a 2-bay desktop NAS with UGREEN NAS OS and RAID 1 support, supporting up to 64TB total capacity, in the $100 to $200 tier. Large capacity ceilings matter when you plan to swap in bigger drives over the years: the enclosure then outlasts the first set of disks.

It ranks sixth because it is a lower-cost model than the DXP2800 and lists less hardware detail. The software is newer, and the listing offers few numbers on CPU or RAM, so you are trusting it for light duties.

Choose it if you want room for large drives later without changing the enclosure. Skip it if you want proven software or app-heavy performance. Drives are sold separately, and a 64TB ceiling is a promise about future drives, not a claim about speed today.

products.name: Asustor Drivestor 2 Gen 2 (AS1202T) 2-Bay NAS
products.verdict: A budget NAS with 2.5GbE and a quad core CPU.
products.description:
The Asustor Drivestor 2 Gen 2 has a quad-core 1.7GHz CPU, 2.5GbE networking, 1GB of soldered DDR4 RAM and 4K media server support in a 2-bay diskless chassis, in the $100 to $200 tier. For plain file sharing and backup, that is a fair mix at a low price.

It ranks seventh because 1GB of RAM is thin for apps, and soldered memory means you cannot add more later. It is aimed at backup and file serving, and a user who wants containers will run out of room.

Buy it if budget is tight and needs are simple, such as backing up laptops and sharing documents. Skip it if you run many apps. The 4K media support suits a single stream, but do not expect heavy transcoding from 1GB.

products.name: Synology DS725+ Expandable NAS (2-Bay Diskless)
products.verdict: Upgradeable RAM and expansion room, at the top price tier.
products.description:
The Synology DS725+ is a Plus-series 2-bay diskless NAS with upgradeable DDR4 RAM, expansion through Synology expansion units and DSM software, in the $500 and up tier. It is aimed at private cloud and small business use, and it is the only pick here that grows with you.

It ranks last only because of price. Most home offices do not need more than the DS223 provides, and the DS725+ asks for a premium that only pays back when you add memory or expansion units.

Choose it for a business that will outgrow two bays, or for one that will run several services on DSM. Skip it if you only back up files. Drives are sold separately, so total cost climbs further once you add two NAS-rated disks.

whatMatters.detail: RAID 1 writes the same data to both drives, so one can fail without data loss. You only get the capacity of one drive. It is not a backup, because deletions mirror too. Check for RAID 1 support in the title or specs, and keep a second copy offsite or in the cloud, because mirroring protects against a dead drive and nothing else.

Diskless means no drives are included, so you must buy two NAS-rated drives. Budget for this on top of the enclosure. Look for the word diskless in the title. Drive choice matters as much as the box, since cheap desktop drives are not designed for continuous operation, and a mismatched pair makes rebuilds slower.

RAM affects apps and containers. Some units solder RAM so it cannot be upgraded, as on the DS223 and the Asustor. The QNAP TS-264 includes 8GB, and the DS725+ takes upgradeable DDR4. Check the RAM line before buying, and note that the TS-216G lists none, so ask before assuming it can run apps.

2.5GbE is faster than gigabit but needs a 2.5GbE switch and computers to benefit. Without them, it runs at gigabit. Check the LAN spec on the listing, and confirm that your router, switch and PC all support the faster speed before paying for it, because the cables need to be rated for it too.

DSM, QTS, TOS and UGREEN NAS OS differ in polish. Synology's DSM is easiest, and the others offer more hardware for the money. Read the OS name on the listing, then judge who will manage the NAS, because poor software costs more time than weak hardware. Try the demo of each interface if the maker offers one.

faq.a: No, all are diskless. Buy two NAS-rated drives separately. A cheap desktop drive may fail sooner under continuous use, so budget for the right kind from the start and buy two of the same capacity.

Treating RAID 1 as a backup. It mirrors deletions, so a mistaken delete or ransomware hits both drives. Keep a second copy elsewhere, whichever of these NAS you choose, and test a restore at least once a year.

faq.q: Is the Plus series worth it over the DS223?
faq.a: Only if you need upgradeable RAM and expansion. The DS725+ costs far more than the DS223, so a home office that backs up files gets little extra from it and could spend the difference on larger drives.

faq.q: How do I set one up?
faq.a: Install the drives, power on and follow the setup wizard in the browser. The Synology DSM wizard is the friendliest, while TOS and QTS take a little longer. Set a strong admin password and disable default accounts before putting files on it.

faq.q: How do I maintain a NAS?
faq.a: Keep firmware updated and check drive health regularly. A mirrored array only protects you if you notice a failing drive, so enable notifications on the DS223 or any other model, and replace a failing drive promptly rather than waiting for the second to fail.

faq.q: Can I run a media server?
faq.a: The Asustor lists 4K media server support, and the QNAP TS-264 suits Plex-style apps with 8GB of RAM. For heavy transcoding, the TERRAMASTER's quad-core Intel CPU has more headroom, though TOS software is less polished.

finalTake: Buy the Synology DS223 if you are new to NAS and mostly need backup. Take the UGREEN DXP2800 for media work, the QNAP TS-264 for apps and containers, and the DS725+ if the office will outgrow two bays. Budget for two NAS-rated drives, and never treat RAID 1 as a backup.
